title: 12  Measurements in real space
text:
12.1 A simple description of \(g(r)\)
In the theory part of the course you have been introduced formally to the radial distribution function \(g(r)\) and seen how it is a useful description of the arrangement of particles in a disordered system. In particular, in the absence of the long range periodic order that is associated with crystalline materials it is one of the first things we wish to find for liquid or glassy material. In our examples we assume that we are looking at a uniform and isotropic material, that is, there is no preferred direction in the material and no density variations on length scales much greater than the particle size. That is, macroscopically the material appears is of uniform density. It is also possible to give a more general definition \(g(\bf{r})\) where we recognise that there is some preferred orientation of the atoms around each other in the material but we will not consider it here.
In layman’s terms the radial distribution function is often described loosely as the probability of finding another particle at a distance from a particle at the origin. If we think about it this way we must remember that \(g(r)\) is a statistical function so what we are really trying to express is the average of this distribution taking each atom in the material in turn as the ‘origin’. Expressed in this way you might worry about what this means for atoms on the ‘edge’. Normally this is not a concern for large samples, but beware about the definition of \(g(r)\)if you start approaching ‘nano-sized’ materials.
A better definition is that \(g(r)\) represents the deviation from the mean particle density, normalised to one, as you move outward from a particle at the origin. It can be mathematically formulated as \[
g(r)=\frac{1}{4\pi r^2\rho}\left\langle \sum_{i\neq0}\delta\!\left(r-r_i\right)\right\rangle,
\] where \(\rho=N/V\) is the average number density, \(r_i\) is the distance of particle \(i\) from the reference particle, and \(\langle\cdots\rangle\) denotes an average over all reference particles. Note that we assumed that this function only depends on the modulus \(r=\left|\mathbf{r}\right|\), i.e., that the material is isotropic. This is not always the case, but if the material is translationally invariant, then this second-order correlation function stil only depends on \(\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r_i}\), and not on the choice of the reference particle. This means that a straightforward generalization is \(g(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\rho}\left\langle \sum_{i\neq0}\delta\!\left(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r_i}\right)\right\rangle\). This generalized relationship will be useful in the next session.
At large \(r\) we expect this to equate to a constant, related to the mean particle density of the material. When properly normalised to the mean density \(g(r) _{r\rightarrow \infty} \rightarrow 1\). The figure below shows the key features of a typical radial distribution function.
Points to note are

title: 12  Measurements in real space
text:
that \(g(r) = 0\) for distances below a characteristic cutoff distance (also referred to as the exclusion zone). Since particles occupy a finite volume and their positions are defined by their centres, two particles cannot approach more closely than a certain minimum distance. In dense systems such as liquids, this minimum distance is often identified with the particle diameter. However, the definition of particle diameter is not always straightforward, and might differ from this value, particularly in crystalline solids.
\(g(r)\) typically rises from 0 to give a ‘first peak’. The position of this peak is referred to as the nearest neighbour distance. (NB. it is not the same as the diameter of the particles).
After the nearest neighbour peak, \(g(r)\) typically dips below the mean density and is characterised by damped oscillating peaks and troughs until \(g(r)\) reaches the constant mean density.







NoteFor the curious and rigorous: from the pair correlation function to the radial distribution function





The most curious and/or mathematically rigorous of you might wonder how the \(4\pi r^2\) appears when assuming that the pair correlation function applies to an isotropic material. Let’s start from its most general expression:
\[
g(\mathbf r)
=
\frac{1}{\rho}
\left\langle
\sum_{i\neq0}
\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_i)
\right\rangle.
\]
To connect this expression to the radial distribution function, we must average over all directions while keeping the distance \(r=|\mathbf{r}|\) fixed:
\[
g(r)
=
\frac{1}{4\pi}
\int g(\mathbf r)\,d\Omega,
\]
where
\[
d\Omega=\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi.
\]
Substituting the definition of \(g(\mathbf r)\) gives
\[
g(r)
=
\frac{1}{4\pi\rho}
\left\langle
\sum_{i\neq0}
\int d\Omega\,
\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_i)
\right\rangle.
\]
The key question is therefore how to express the three-dimensional Dirac delta in spherical coordinates.
Recall that under a change of variables, a Dirac delta acquires the inverse Jacobian. In one dimension,
\[
\delta(f(x))
=
\sum_i
\frac{\delta(x-x_i)}
{\left|f'(x_i)\right|},
\]
where the \(x_i\) are the roots of \(f(x)\).
More generally, if a coordinate transformation \((x,y,z)\mapsto(u,v,w)\) has Jacobian \(J\), then
\[
\delta(x-x_0)\,
\delta(y-y_0)\,
\delta(z-z_0)
=
\frac{
\delta(u-u_0)\,
\delta(v-v_0)\,
\delta(w-w_0)
}{
|J|
}.
\]
For spherical coordinates,
\[
(x,y,z)
=
(r\sin\theta\cos\phi,
\; r\sin\theta\sin\phi,
\; r\cos\theta),
\]
whose Jacobian is
\[
J=r^2\sin\theta.
\]
Therefore
\[
d^3r
=
r^2\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi,
\]
and the three-dimensional delta becomes
\[
\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_i)
=
\frac{
\delta(r-r_i)\,
\delta(\theta-\theta_i)\,
\delta(\phi-\phi_i)
}{
r^2\sin\theta
}.
\]
Substituting this result into the angular average yields
\[
\int d\Omega\,
\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_i)
=
\int
\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi\,
\frac{
\delta(r-r_i)\,
\delta(\theta-\theta_i)\,
\delta(\phi-\phi_i)
}{
r^2\sin\theta
}.
\]
The factor of \(\sin\theta\) from the solid-angle element cancels the \(\sin\theta\) in the denominator:
\[
=
\frac{\delta(r-r_i)}{r^2}
\int d\theta\,
\delta(\theta-\theta_i)
\int d\phi\,
\delta(\phi-\phi_i).
\]
Using the defining property of the Dirac delta,
\[
\int d\theta\,\delta(\theta-\theta_i)=1,
\qquad
\int d\phi\,\delta(\phi-\phi_i)=1,
\]
we obtain
\[
\int d\Omega\,
\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_i)
=
\frac{\delta(r-r_i)}{r^2}.
\]
Substituting this back into the definition of \(g(r)\) gives
\[
g(r)
=
\frac{1}{4\pi r^2\rho}
\left\langle
\sum_{i\neq0}
\delta(r-r_i)
\right\rangle.
\]
This is the standard expression for the radial distribution function.
The factor \(4\pi r^2\) therefore has a purely geometric origin: it arises from the Jacobian \(r^2\sin\theta\) associated with transforming the three-dimensional Dirac delta from Cartesian to spherical coordinates and then integrating over all directions.

title: 12  Measurements in real space
section: 12.2 How to we measure \(g(r)\) directly for a material?
text:
12.2 How to we measure \(g(r)\) directly for a material?
In order to measure \(g(r)\) directly, we need to obtain a 3D (unless we are looking at a 2D system) image of the material in which all the particle coordinates \(r_i(x,y,z)\) can be obtained. Although some modern techniques can obtain images with atomic resolution (for example scanning tunneling microscopy) they are mostly limited to surface imaging and not suitable for studying liquids (where atoms are moving around). Although some X-ray and electron microscopy techniques (see for example ptychography) can produce atomic scale resolution (using coherent imaging techniques) these are again largely confined to 2D surfaces and are again not suitable for atomic liquids.

A powerful alternative is to study colloidal suspensions, in which the constituent particles are typically hundreds of nanometres to several micrometres in size. Because these particles are many orders of magnitude larger than atoms, they can often be imaged directly in three dimensions using optical techniques. Colloids therefore provide an excellent model system for investigating disorder, phase transitions, and particle-scale dynamics in condensed matter. In particular, confocal microscopy makes it possible to reconstruct the three-dimensional coordinates of individual particles, and even to track their motion over time. As a result, many concepts that are difficult to probe directly in atomic liquids can be studied experimentally in colloidal systems. In the following sections, we will examine some of the techniques used to extract particle positions and characterize their structure and dynamics. We will manipulate real microscopic images from colloidal suspensions at the end of this course.

title: 12  Measurements in real space
text:
12.3 The structure of colloidal systems
If you ask someone what paint, milk, blood, fog, coffee and ink have in common, they would probably struggle to find a convincing answer. Physically, however, they all belong to the same broad class of materials: colloidal systems.
A colloid consists of a dispersed phase made of particles, droplets or bubbles suspended within a continuous phase. Depending on whether the dispersed and continuous phases are solid, liquid or gas, colloids can take many different forms, ranging from aerosols (fog, smoke) to emulsions (milk, mayonnaise), foams (whipped cream) and particle suspensions (paint, blood).




Various types of colloids depending on the thermodynamic state of dispersed and continuous phase. Pictures represents, from left to right, then from top to bottom : whipped cream, shaving foam, marshmallow, suitcase foam, clouds, liquid spray, mayonnaise, milk, butter, cheese, smoke, suspended dust, coffee, paint, zircon gemstone and selenium ruby (a type of coloured glass).

Despite their diversity, all colloids share a common characteristic: the dispersed objects are small enough to exhibit behaviour that differs markedly from both molecules and macroscopic particles. Their typical size ranges from a few nanometres to a few tens of micrometres. Because of this intermediate size scale, colloidal systems often display unique optical, rheological and transport properties that underpin countless applications in food processing, pharmaceuticals, coatings, printing technologies and environmental science.
A schematic colloidal suspension is shown below. The dispersed particles (phase \(\beta\)) are suspended within a continuous phase (phase \(\alpha\)). At sufficiently small sizes, the particles are continuously bombarded by molecules of the surrounding fluid, giving rise to Brownian motion, the random motion first observed by Robert Brown in 1827.




Typical structure of a colloidal suspension. The colloid is constituted by a continuous (or dispersing) phase, noted \(\alpha\), and a dispersed phase, noted \(\beta\). The radius (or typical size) \(R\) of the suspended particles ranges from between the nanometre and a few hundreds of micrometre. A typical example of Brownian motion is represented in dotted lines for the central particle. The P'eclet number, sometimes used in the definition of colloids, explicitly depends on the diffusion coefficient of this motion. The Brownian motion results from the interaction between the resulting force from the weight and the buoyancy of the particles \(\vec{P}\) and the random thermodynamic force \(\vec{\xi}\) due to collisions with molecules of the continuous phase, according to Langevin theory.

Some authors define colloidal systems primarily through this Brownian motion. In this view, a suspension is considered colloidal when random thermal motion is significant compared with the tendency of particles to sediment under gravity. A convenient measure of this competition is the Péclet number
\[
Pe=\frac{D}{vL},
\]
where \(D\) is the particle diffusion coefficient, \(v\) a characteristic sedimentation velocity and \(L\) a characteristic length scale. When \(Pe \gg 1\), Brownian diffusion dominates over sedimentation and particles remain well dispersed. For particles suspended in water under ambient conditions, this criterion typically corresponds to particle sizes below roughly one micrometre, in good agreement with the conventional size range of colloidal particles.
In this course we will focus primarily on colloidal suspensions, namely solid particles dispersed in a liquid. For simplicity, we will often model the particles as spherical objects interacting as nearly ideal hard-sphere systems, where particles interact primarily through excluded volume effects. Such systems have become invaluable model materials for investigating phase transitions, crystallisation and glass formation at the particle scale. Although idealised, this description captures many of the fundamental physical phenomena that make colloids attractive model systems for studying phase transitions, crystallisation, glasses and particle-scale organisation.






NoteOne step further: Colloidal stability





In reality, colloidal interactions are much more complex than ideal hard spheres: some practical difficulty immediately arises when attempting to create a colloidal suspension. If spherical particles are simply mixed into a solvent, they rarely remain uniformly dispersed for long. Attractive interactions, particularly van der Waals forces, tend to pull neighbouring particles together, leading to aggregation or flocculation (potentially visible in your coffee cup if you add oat milk in it).
From a thermodynamic perspective, colloidal dispersions are generally only metastable. Without additional stabilising mechanisms, particles progressively aggregate into larger clusters, due to (at least) so-called Van der Waals attraction, eventually resulting in macroscopic phase separation.
To maintain a homogeneous suspension, a repulsive interaction must be introduced to counteract these attractive forces. The most common stabilisation mechanism is electrostatic stabilisation. When particles acquire a surface charge, counter-ions in the surrounding liquid form an electrical double layer around each particle. As two particles approach one another, overlap of these double layers generates a repulsive force that can prevent aggregation.




Illustration of the ionic double layer around a charged colloidal particle. Picture modified from Adapted from T. Cosgrove, Colloid Science: Principles, Methods and Applications, John Wiley & Sons, 2010.

The thickness of the diffuse ionic layer is characterised by the so-called Debye length, which depends strongly on the salt concentration of the solvent. By modifying parameters such as pH or ionic strength, it is therefore possible to tune the balance between attraction and repulsion and control the stability of the suspension.
Another widely used approach is steric stabilisation. In this case, polymer chains are grafted onto the particle surfaces, creating a protective “hairy” layer. As particles approach each other, compression of these polymer layers becomes energetically unfavourable, generating a strong repulsion that suppresses aggregation.

title: 12  Measurements in real space
section: 12.4 How to we obtain \(g(r)\) and information about coordination from colloid systems.
text:
12.4 How to we obtain \(g(r)\) and information about coordination from colloid systems.
If we have our ideal colloid there are several things we may wish to control. For example, what is the size of the particles (there will be a tendency for large particles to sediment), are the particles all the same size (polydispersivity), can we make systems with different shapes (e.g. ovoid), can we make systems with mixed particle sizes, can we introduce directional interactions (Janus particles) and how do you control the number density of the particles (the density of the particles is the crucial parameter for describing the hard sphere phase diagram)? These all pose theoretical and experimental difficulties of their own. Finally, once we’ve prepared our colloid with a controlled density … how do we study its structure (and dynamics)?

title: 12  Measurements in real space
text:
12.5 Confocal microscopy.
There are a few further steps we need to achieve to be able to measure and track the positions of the particles in our hard sphere colloid. Firstly, it is important that the particles are transparent, otherwise, we will not be able to see into the depth of the sample and secondly we need to match, as closely as possible, the refractive index of the solvent. If we don’t do this the difference in refractive index will mean light is quickly scattered in all directions meaning we will just have an opaque material. However, by making the particles all but invisible how to we determine their positions? The trick is to include a fluorescent dye their centre. When illuminated with the correct wavelength of light (using a laser) the particles will glow. This works well but how do we measure the positions of the particles in 3D. The answer is to use a confocal microscope as illustrated below (figure take from Royall et. al.2024).



In the confocal microscope laser light is passed through a small pinhole and then brought to focus at a point in the sample by a lens, known as the condenser lens. The fluorescent light coming back from the illuminated samples is then focused by the objective lens (which in this case is the same lens as the condenser) and the microscopy image is obtained by the camera. However, although the laser light is brought to a tight focus in the sample there are nevertheless still regions that are illuminated by the laser that, under normal circumstances, would also bring unwanted light into the camera. The key point of the confocal system is that a second pinhole is placed precisely at the focus (hence confocal) of the objective lens for the light coming from the sample. The effect of this pinhole is to reduce the volume of the sample that is illuminated and then seen by the camera. The method is good enough that the fluorescence from individual particles can be observed clearly and the ultimate ability to resolve the individual particles is given by the diffraction limit imposed by the wavelength of the laser light used. (There are also ways in which this has been overcome to an extent in practical systems). The figures below, also taken from Royall et. al. 2024 show examples of confocal images used to map out the phase diagram of the hard sphere system.



Note, moving the sample up and down changes the ‘z’ direction and a three dimensional image may be obtained by ‘stacking’ vertically scanned 2D images.
Once the particles positions have been determined it is possible to plot \(g(r)\) for the different packing densities to show how it varies over the phase diagram as shown below



The early attempts at understanding the packing of particles in disordered materials came to te conclusion that 5 fold coordination (inconsistent with the long range order required for crystals) was the characteristic of simple dense packed structures. In the same spirit as these early experiments the results from confocal imaging have allowed the prevalence of different types of local ordering to be investigated. This leads to the mapping out the \(\textit{topological cluster distribution}\) (i.e. the different types of local structure) that occur in the system. As noted before, these higher order correlations may be calculated from the particle positions (once we have them) but cannot be determined unambiguously from measurements of \(g(r)\) alone.



These are just a few examples of the areas studied using colloids and confocal microscopy techqniues.

title: 12  Measurements in real space
text:
12.6 Calculation of \(g(r)\) directly from simulation
Although simulation is not strictly an experimental method, it is neither a truly theoretical method either. This said, from the experimentalist point of view, especially in the case of the colloind systems studied above, they provide a direct comparison in real space with the data. As such the experiemntal results are an important check of the veracity of the simulation methods especially with regard to the application of for example theoretical potentials. The simulation methods naturally exploit the interaction of the particles in real space (we know the positions of the particles and we calculate how they move under the influence of the interparticle forces. Hence, it is quite straight forward to compare the real space configurations measured in experiment with the particle coordinates in the simulation. The comparison between the experiment and simulation and the level of agreement that can be achieved can be strikingly seen in the comparison of \(g(r)\) for hard spheres shown above. Simulations however are not the answer to everything. They get more and more computer intensive as larger numbers of particles are included and the time scales over which they are carried out are extremely short compared to those in experiments. The latter is a particular issue with studies of the glass transition (as always) where the physical processes taking place may occur over a very wide range of timescales.
The comparison of simulation results with experimental diffraction data is more difficult. Diffraction experiments are a reciprocal space measurement and to compare to simulation we need to work out the corresponding real space (\(g(r)\) ) distributions. Hence when comparing experiment with simulation we have to choose whether to transform our reciprocal space data to real space (with associated problems) or convert the real space data from our simulations to reciprocal space for comparison (that also has problems). This is the subject of the next part of this course.

title: 12  Measurements in real space
section: 12.7 Practical Exercise: Determining Structure from the Radial Distribution Function
text:
12.7 Practical Exercise: Determining Structure from the Radial Distribution Function
In this exercise, you will use the provided Python code to calculate the radial distribution function, \(g(r)\), from a set of particle coordinates. By applying the same analysis to different systems, you will discover how \(g(r)\) can distinguish between gases, liquids, and solids, and how quantitative structural information can be extracted from experimental and simulation data.

12.7.1 Learning Objectives
By the end of this exercise, you should be able to:

Run a Python script that calculates \(g(r)\) from particle coordinates.
Understand the purpose of each section of the code.
Interpret the main features of a radial distribution function.
Identify whether a sample is a gas, liquid, or solid from its \(g(r)\).
Estimate:

the closest distance of approach,
the average nearest-neighbour distance,
the cutoff distance defining the first coordination shell,
the coordination number.





12.7.2 Obtaining and Visualising the Data
If not already done, download the coordinate and code files from the shared University of Bristol folder:
Data folder: Download the coordinate datasets
The folder contains particle coordinates for several systems:

Graphite (perfect structure)
Graphite at room temperature
Silicon (perfect structure)
Silicon at room temperature
Water
A theoretical Lennard-Jones Gas (with arbitrary length units!)

Each file contains the \((x,y,z)\) coordinates of all particles in the sample.
Choose one dataset to analyse. Later in the exercise you will compare your results with your classmates having worked on different systems. It is a good idea to coordinate with one or two of your direct neighbours to work on different datasets.



12.7.3 Running the Code
Locate the line in the Python script that loads the particle coordinates:
positions = np.loadtxt("filename.txt")
Replace the filename by one of the supplied datasets and execute the script.
Let’s review the code main steps and make sure we understand what information is being calculated.

12.7.3.1 Loading the Coordinates
positions = np.loadtxt(...)
N = len(positions)

positions contains a table whose various rows are the (x,y,z) components of the particles in the sample
N is the number of lines, i.e. the number of particles




12.7.3.2 Determining the Simulation Volume
The code determines the dimensions of the simulation box and estimates its volume, which is necessary to compute the number density of the particles:
xmin = np.min(positions[:,0])
xmax = np.max(positions[:,0])

...

volume = Lx * Ly * Lz



12.7.3.3 Calculating the Number Density
The particle number density is calculated as
\[
\rho=\frac{N}{V}.
\]


12.7.3.4 Questions

What physical quantity does \(\rho\) represent?
Would you expect \(\rho\) to be larger for a gas or a liquid?




12.7.3.5 Dividing Distances into Bins
The code creates a histogram of interparticle distances.
n_bins = 100


12.7.3.6 Questions

What is the purpose of the histogram bins?
What would happen if very few bins were used?
What would happen if an extremely large number of bins were used?




12.7.3.7 Measuring Pair Distances
The code loops over all particle pairs and calculates their separation:
r = np.sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy + dz*dz)



12.7.3.8 Normalisation
The histogram is converted into the radial distribution function,
\[
g(r),
\]
by comparing the measured number of neighbours with the number expected in a perfectly random distribution.




12.7.4 First Analysis of Your Graph
Run the code and examine the resulting plot.

12.7.4.1 Questions

Why is \(g(r)\) zero at short distances?
At what value of \(r\) does it first become non-zero?
Is there a clear first peak?
Are there several peaks?
Does the curve eventually approach \(g(r)=1\)?

Discuss your observations with your neighbours, and compare with their own systems.




12.7.5 Finite-Size Effects and Periodic Boundary Conditions
Before moving on to identifying the phase of your material, take a careful look at your \(g(r)\) curve.

12.7.5.1 An Observation
For an ideal liquid or gas, we would expect
\[
g(r) \rightarrow 1
\]
after \(r\) exceeds a few particle diameters, since particles become effectively uncorrelated when they are sufficiently far apart. It should also happen for crystals, but often at distances bigger than what can be observed experimentally while still resolving the first neighbours structure.
However, you may notice that your calculated \(g(r)\) for the liquid and gas datasets does not seem to approach 1 at large \(r\).


12.7.5.2 Think About It
Why might the measured \(g(r)\) fail to reach 1, even though the system should behave like a liquid or gas?
Discuss your ideas with your neighbours before continuing.



12.7.5.3 A Clue in the Code
In the distance-calculation section of the script, you may have noticed the following commented-out lines:
# For a gas or liquid, implement periodic boundary conditions
# (minimum-image convention)

# dx = dx - Lx * round(dx / Lx)
# dy = dy - Ly * round(dy / Ly)
# dz = dz - Lz * round(dz / Lz)
These lines implement periodic boundary conditions using the minimum-image convention.
The idea is to treat the simulation box as if it were repeated infinitely in every direction.
A particle leaving one side of the box immediately re-enters from the opposite side.
When calculating distances, we therefore measure the shortest possible separation between two particles, taking into account all neighbouring copies of the simulation box.



12.7.5.4 Try It Yourself
You might first want to change the variables OutputName and GraphName to be able to compare both outputs.
Uncomment the three lines:
dx = dx - Lx * round(dx / Lx)
dy = dy - Ly * round(dy / Ly)
dz = dz - Lz * round(dz / Lz)
and run the code again on your dataset.

Does \(g(r)\) now approach 1 at large distances?
Which result should you consider as correct and why?




12.7.5.5 Discussion
The answer is not necessarily the same as for liquids and gases.
For liquids and gases, periodic boundary conditions are often essential because they reduce finite-size effects and better represent an effectively infinite bulk material, provided their structure is not correlated over the length of the box.
For crystals, however, the coordinates correspond to a specific finite arrangement of atoms. Artificially repeating the simulation box may introduce correlations that were not directly present in the original dataset. Whether periodic boundaries should be used therefore depends on what physical system the coordinates are intended to represent.



12.7.6 Identifying the Phase
The overall shape of \(g(r)\) reveals the state of matter.

12.7.6.1 Typical Gas

Weak or no pronounced peaks.
\(g(r)\approx1\) over most distances.
Little spatial order.



12.7.6.2 Typical Liquid

Strong first peak.
Smaller secondary peaks.
Oscillations gradually decay towards 1.



12.7.6.3 Typical Crystal / Solid

Many sharp peaks.
Well defined neighbour shells.
Long-range order visible over large distances. (\(g(r)\approx1\) might not ne observable over realistic datasets)



12.7.6.4 Questions

Does your sample behave as a gas, liquid, or solid?
Compare your graph with those obtained by neighbouring classmates.
What are the main differences between the three classes of materials?





12.7.7 Quantitative Information from \(g(r)\)
One of the strengths of the radial distribution function is that it contains quantitative structural information.

12.7.7.1 Closest Distance of Approach
Estimate the distance at which \(g(r)\) first becomes significantly different from zero. What is the closest distance of approach in your sample?



12.7.7.2 Nearest-Neighbour Distance
Locate the first maximum of \(g(r)\).
The position of this first peak corresponds to the most probable nearest-neighbour distance.
What is the nearest-neighbour distance in your sample?



12.7.7.3 Cutoff Distance of the First Coordination Shell
Locate the first minimum immediately after the first peak.
This is commonly used to define the boundary of the first coordination shell. What value do you obtain for the cutoff distance?



12.7.7.4 Coordination Number (if time allows)
The coordination number is the average number of neighbours contained within the first shell.
It can be obtained from
\[
N_c=4\pi\rho \int_0^{r_c}g(r)r^2dr,
\]
where \(r_c\) is the position of the first minimum.

Estimate the coordination number of your sample.
How does your result compare with those obtained by neighbouring groups?
Which sample appears to have the largest coordination number?





12.7.8 Extension Activity: Effect of Temperature
Analyse both:

Silicon at 0 K
Silicon at Room Temperature

Compare the resulting radial distribution functions.

How does temperature affect the height of the peaks?
How does temperature affect the width of the peaks?
Does long-range order disappear completely?
What physical mechanism explains the observed differences?




12.7.9 Conclusions
Before moving on, make sure that you can confidently:

Distinguish a gas, liquid, and solid from a radial distribution function.
Estimate the closest distance of approach.
Determine the average nearest-neighbour distance.
Identify the cutoff distance of the first coordination shell.
Estimate the coordination number.




12.7.10 Data Sources
The coordinate datasets used in this exercise were generated from the following sources:

Graphite and Silicon: crystal structures obtained from the Materials Project database, with Gaussian positional noise added to mimic thermal motion.
Liquid configurations (water): are obtained from the Zenodo public database published along Cassone, G., Martelli, F. Electrofreezing of liquid water at ambient conditions. Nat Commun 15, 1856 (2024)
Gas configurations: obtained from running the simulations from Alexei Korolev’s GitHub

Please acknowledge these sources if you use the datasets outside this practical session.

title: 12  Measurements in real space
section: 12.8 In summary: What can we learn from \(g(r)\)?
text:
12.8 In summary: What can we learn from \(g(r)\)?

12.8.1 The exclusion zone
A characteristic feature of the radial distribution function is the presence of an exclusion zone, corresponding to a range of distances for which \(g(r)=0\). This reflects the fact that particles occupy a finite volume and that their positions are defined by the locations of their centres. Consequently, two particles cannot approach each other more closely than a certain minimum distance, making the probability of finding particle centres within this range effectively zero. In dense systems such as liquids, this minimum distance is often taken to be approximately equal to the particle diameter. More generally, however, the exclusion zone should be interpreted as the closest distance of approach between neighbouring particles. The precise relationship between this distance and the particle diameter depends on the nature of the interactions and the structure of the material, and is not always straightforward, particularly in crystalline solids.


12.8.2 Average first neighbour distance
A second important feature of the radial distribution function is the presence of a first peak. Starting from the exclusion zone, where \(g(r)=0\), the function rises rapidly and reaches a maximum at a characteristic distance. This peak corresponds to the most probable separation between a particle and its nearest neighbours and is therefore referred to as the nearest-neighbour distance. Physically, it reflects the preferred local arrangement of particles within the material. It is important to note that the nearest-neighbour distance is generally not the same as the particle diameter. While the particle diameter characterises the size of an individual particle, the nearest-neighbour distance is determined by the structure of the system and the interactions between particles, and can therefore be significantly larger than the distance of closest approach.


12.8.3 Peak positions.
The peaks observed in \(g(r)\) correspond to the most common interparticle seperation. For an atomic system, they can typically be associated with chemical bonds and as you move further in \(r\) the \(\textit{medium}\) (i.e. next nearest neighbour …) range ordering. However, we must remember that this is only a pair corrrelation function. It does not \(\it{per~se}\) tell us about for example bond angles. These are formally be obtained from higher order correlation functionz (triplet, …) but these are not obtainable directly from \(g(r)\) itself.
Note. If we have a crystalline material the peaks in \(g(r)\) will be narrow (they will have an intrinsic width at least due to thermal vibration) and at low values of \(r\), \(g(r)\) will be zero between them. However, even in a crystalline material these peaks will start to broaden and get smaller at high \(r\) until, again, \(g(r)\) reaches mean density.


12.8.4 Coordination numbers.
\(g(r)\) is a dimensionless function that normalises to a mean density of one at large \(r\). For a material with a \(\textit{number~density}\), \(\rho_N\), the mean number density at distance \(r\) is hence \(\rho_N g(r)\). A thin spherical shell of thickness \(\Delta r\) at a distance \(r\) will have a volume \(4\pi r^2 \Delta r\) so that the mean number of atoms in the shell will be,
\(4\pi r^2 \rho_N(r) \Delta r\).
Hence the mean number of atoms in a spherical shell of inner radius \(r_1\) and outer radius \(r_2\) will be given by,
\(\bar{n} = 4\pi\rho_N\int_{r1}^{r2}r^2g(r)dr\).
If we define a peak in \(g(r)\) by \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) we call \(n\) the coordination number of the particles in the peak. The coordination number is the average number of neighbours contained within the first shell.



It is important to note that the coordination number is an average (\(g(r)\) is a statistical distribution) and in general will vary particle by particle in the material. It does not have to be integer and unless \(g(r_1)=g(r_2)=0\) it is an ill defined quantity. Nevertheless, it is a commonly quoted number in research papers so it is important to read carefully how it has been caclulated to obtain meaningful conclusions that can be compared to figures in other research work.

title: 12  Measurements in real space
text:
12.9 Dynamics in real space
Confocal microscopy experiments are not only useful for static measurements of \(g(r)\) but also open up the possibility for studying the dynamics of the system (how the particles move over time), that is, measurement of the time dependent pair correlation function \(G(r,t)\) I’ll not say much about dynamics in this lecture, but it is worth mentioning it as it is a very active research field. Needless to say the process involves taking confocal images of the particles over time scales in which they will move only slightly from their initial position. With sophisticated software it is then possible to label the particles and track their position and hence coordinates in succesive image frames. This work well if you are in the sweet spot for the measurements but is a challenge, for example in glass transition experiments, where the experimental timescales become longer and longer as you approach the conditions for the glass transition to take place. This is still a very active field.

title: 12  Measurements in real space
text:
12.10 Conclusion and keypoints
In this section we have considered the experimental determination of \(g(r)\).

We have seen that this is not realistically possible for atmonic systems,
we have seen how colloid systems are ideal systems for studying the properties of hard-sphere and closely related systems on the 100nm scale,
we have seen how \(g(r)\) for colloids may be obtained from the coordinates obtained from confocal microscopy,
we have seen how \(g(r)\) and higher order correlations may be obtained from these coordinates,
we have seen how we can extend the confocal microscopy method to study particle dynamics.

title: 13  Measurements in reciprocal space
text:
13.1 Diffraction
In the previous experimental section we saw how measurements of \(g(r)\) may be made by directly finding coordinates of particles in space. We saw how this could be applied to colloidal systems. The optical methods applied are confined to systems at or close to the diffraction limit, that for optical wavelengths is a few hundred nanometres. Another problem that may arise is that \(g(r)\) is a statistical quantity and to obtain meaningful results it must be calculated over a large number of particle positions and care must be taken to ensure that the system under study is homogeneous.
In order to determine \(g(r)\) directly in a similar way for atomic and molecular systems we would need to use wavelengths that are much less than the atomic size, that is beyond X-ray wavelengths. This is not practical. In contrast, it is possible to image at the atomic scale using electron microscopy. However, in this case it is not possible to image in the bulk in a similar way to confocal microscopy and studies are largely limited to 2D surfaces. Hence, most studies at this scale are based on diffraction methods - the topic of this part of the course.
Optically, you are aware from your study of waves that diffraction effects occur when the scale of the structure is of the same order of the wavelength of light. The same principle applies for atomic scales which means diffraction needs wavelengths around 0.1 nanometres (or 1 Å) for atomic scale studies.
0.1 nm is in the X-ray regime but it’s also accessible with thermal neutrons (~ 300K is approximately 0.18 nm) or electrons. (Exercise. Calculate the energy of a photon, neutron and electron corresponding to a wavelength of 0.1 nm.).
So how do we use diffraction in disordered systems to obtain structural information such as \(g(r)\)?

title: 13  Measurements in reciprocal space
section: 13.2 The structure factor - a simple approach.
text:
13.2 The structure factor - a simple approach.
We will not use a rigorous approach to diffraction (that requires quantum mechanics) but we will approach the relationship between the scattering of x-rays, neutrons and electrons by atoms by considering the following simple picture, with \(\phi\) the relevant wavefunction. We note that we haven’t included the strength or the specific way in which the atoms scatter at this point but have assumed an incoming quantum plane wave is scattered by the atoms. We also assume for the moment that we only have one atom type.



We then wish to understand how the scattered waves from different atoms interfere to give rise to a diffraction pattern (for example scattered intensity vs. angle). Let’s write \(\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{k'}-\mathbf{k}\) the scattering vector.



We begin with the so-called Born approximation: let’s consider that the incident and scattered radiation are represented by plane waves, and only single-scattering events are considered. That is, each atom scatters only the incident wave, while the contribution of waves scattered by other atoms is neglected. Under these assumptions, Under these assumptions, the structure factor (note that this differs from the conventional crystallographic definition of the structure factor), also called interference function, especially in experimental contexts, can be written as



We note that \(N\) is just a normalizing factor to give the scattering per atom and that for a liquid (or any isotropic material) we need to take the spherical average of this function to return a function \(S(Q)\) that is isotropic (the same in all directions). (NB. This latter step would not be taken, in for example representing the scattering from a liquid crystal, where we know there is an orientation of the molecules in the liquid - the director - even though there is still liquid like disorder in the other directions).
A more formal derivation of the structure factor obtained in a scattering experiment for a single element may be found in Fischer et al. (2006) and may be written in terms of the differential scattering cross-section, \(\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\), defined as the scattered intensity per unit solid angle divided by the incident flux. The scattered intensity measured at a detector a distance \(L\) from the sample is related to the differential cross-section through
\[
I_{\rm sc}(L,\theta,\phi) =\frac{I_{\rm inc}}{L^2} \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega},\]
where \(I_{\rm inc}\) is the incident intensity and \(L\) is the sample-to-detector distance:
\[\frac{1}{N} \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = b_{coh}^2 S(Q)+b_{incoh}^2,\]
for neutrons where \(b_{coh}\) is the coherent scattering length of the element and \(b_{incoh}\) is the incoherent scattering length that arises due to the difference in scattering by the nucleus when its nuclear spin (if it has a spin) is aligned or anti-aligned with the neutron and/or when it is different due to the nuclear scattering arising from different isotopes of the same element.
For the case of X-rays the corresponding quantity, in its simplest form is,
\[\frac{1}{N} \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}=f(Q)^2 S(Q)\]
where \(f\) is the scatterig form factor of an atom, and we note this is after corrections for the effects of polarization of the x-ray beam in the incident and scattered beam has been made.



From the figure we note the important difference between the neutron and X-ray diffraction patterns. At large values of \(Q\) the neutron diffraction cross-section tends to a constant value \(b^2_{coh}+b^2_{incoh}\) whereas for X-rays we see that the diffraction tends to zero at large \(Q\) due to the \(Q\) dependence of the X-ray form factor. The physical origin of this effect is that for neutrons it is the nucleus (with a size of a few femtometres) that is the scattering object whereas for X-rays it is the electron cloud around the atom (with dimensions of about a tenth of a nanometer) that is the scattering object. Hence for a thermal neutron (of wavelength 0.18 nm) the atoms in the material act as point scatterers whereas the scattering from X-rays is for an object of roughly the same wavelength. Hence the shape of \(f(Q)\) reflects the distribution of the electrons around the atom. This \(Q\) dependence of the form factor has important consequences when we consider materials composed of more than one element as we shall see shortly.






NoteOptical equivalent





The effect is equivalent in optics to the difference from the diffraction pattern from a grating that is composed of very narrow slits compared to one composed of slit widths on the same scale as their separation cf.
\[I\sim \left(\frac{\sin \alpha}{\alpha}\right)^2\left(\frac{\sin N\beta}{\sin\beta}\right)^2\]



We also note that both \(b\) and \(f(Q)\) should be considered as complex quantities (that give rise to absorption and alter the scattering cross-section close to a neutron resonance or X-ray absorption edge).
Hence, provided we are able to make the experimental corrections we can see that, at least for a single element, \(S(Q)\) for the liquid or glass may be obtained directly.
Here are some images of some typical X-ray and neutron diffractometers at the ILL and ESRF central facilities.

title: 13  Measurements in reciprocal space
section: 13.3 The relationship between \(S(Q)\) and \(g(r)\) for a disordered material.
text:
13.3 The relationship between \(S(Q)\) and \(g(r)\) for a disordered material.

13.3.1 Conceptual Summary
The description above gives insight into the origins of the interference (diffraction) effects observed from a disordered arrangement of scatterers. There is a direct sine Fourier transform pair relationship between the radial distribution function \(g(r)\) and the structure factor \(S(Q)\) for the material and is as follows.
\[S(Q)=1+\frac{4\pi\rho}{Q}\int_0^{\infty}r(g(r)-1)\sin(Qr)dr\]
and
\[g(r)=1+\frac{1}{2\pi\rho r}\int_0^{\infty}Q(S(Q)-1)\sin(Qr)dQ\]
Again, we note that these quantities do not depend on the nature of the scattering. Hence, by measuring \(S(Q)\) we can in principle obtain \(g(r)\).






NoteA more complete demonstration





Starting from the definition of the structure factor,
\[
S(\mathbf Q)=\frac{1}{N}\left|\sum_{n=1}^{N} e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot\mathbf R_n}\right|^2,
\]
expand the square modulus:
\[
S(\mathbf Q)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot(\mathbf R_i-\mathbf R_j)}.
\]
Separating the diagonal (\(i=j\)) and off-diagonal (\(i\neq j\)) terms, and rewriting the \(1/N\) sum on \(j\) as an average
\[
S(\mathbf Q)=\left\langle 1+\sum_{i\neq j}e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot(\mathbf R_i-\mathbf R_j)}\right\rangle,
\]
which gives
\[
S(\mathbf Q)=1+\left\langle\sum_{i\neq j}e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot(\mathbf R_i-\mathbf R_j)}\right\rangle.
\]
For a homogeneous system, fix one particle at the origin (always set \(\mathbf{r}_j=\mathbf{0}\)) and introduce the pair-correlation function
\[
g(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{\rho}\left\langle\sum_{i\neq0}\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_i)\right\rangle,
\]
so that
\[
\rho\,g(\mathbf r)=\left\langle\sum_{i\neq0}\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_i)\right\rangle.
\]
Using this definition, the off-diagonal term can be rewritten as
\[
\frac{1}{N}\left\langle\sum_{i\neq j}e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot(\mathbf R_i-\mathbf R_j)}\right\rangle=\rho\int g(\mathbf r)\,e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot\mathbf r}\,d^3r.
\]
Hence
\[
S(\mathbf Q)=1+\rho\int g(\mathbf r)\,e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot\mathbf r}\,d^3r.
\]
which is almost the desired relation. However, since \(g(\mathbf r)\to1\) as \(r\to\infty\), the Fourier transform contains the contribution of the uniform background density, which produces a Dirac delta at \(\mathbf Q=0\). Removing this trivial contribution yields
\[
S(\mathbf Q)=1+\rho\int[g(\mathbf r)-1]\,e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot\mathbf r}\,d^3r.
\]
for \(\mathbf{Q}\neq 0\), showing that the structure factor is the Fourier transform of the so-called total correlation function \(h(\mathbf r)=g(\mathbf r)-1\).

13.3.1.1 Isotropic Case
For an isotropic material,
\[
g(\mathbf r)=g(r),\qquad S(\mathbf Q)=S(Q).
\]
Choose spherical coordinates with the polar axis along \(\mathbf Q\). Then
\[
\mathbf Q\cdot\mathbf r = Qr\cos\theta,
\]
and
\[
d^3r=r^2\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi.
\]
Substituting into the Fourier transform gives
\[
S(Q)-1=\rho\int_0^\infty[g(r)-1]\,r^2\,dr\int_0^{2\pi}d\phi\int_0^\pi e^{iQr\cos\theta}\sin\theta\,d\theta.
\]
The azimuthal integral is
\[
\int_0^{2\pi}d\phi=2\pi.
\]
For the polar integral, let
\[
u=\cos\theta,\qquad du=-\sin\theta\,d\theta.
\]
Then
\[
\int_0^\pi e^{iQr\cos\theta}\sin\theta\,d\theta=\int_{-1}^{1}e^{iQru}\,du.
\]
Evaluating,
\[
\int_{-1}^{1}e^{iQru}\,du=\left[\frac{e^{iQru}}{iQr}\right]_{-1}^{1}=\frac{e^{iQr}-e^{-iQr}}{iQr}=\frac{2\sin(Qr)}{Qr}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\int d\Omega\,e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot\mathbf r}=2\pi\frac{2\sin(Qr)}{Qr}=4\pi\frac{\sin(Qr)}{Qr}.
\]
Substituting back,
\[
\boxed{S(Q)=1+4\pi\rho\int_0^\infty[g(r)-1]\frac{\sin(Qr)}{Qr}\,r^2\,dr.}
\]

title: 13  Measurements in reciprocal space
text:
13.4 Practical points
In practice it is not possible to measure the complete \(S(Q)\) function in an experiment. Apart from statistical and systematic uncertainties in the measurements, we see the maximum value of \(Q\) that can be measured is determined by the maximum scattering angle and the wavelength of the x-ray, neutron etc. So for \(2\theta= 180^\circ\) (\(\pi\)), the maximum possible scattering angle, we obtain \(Q_{\max}=\frac{4\pi}{\lambda}\), where \(\lambda\) is the wavelength. There is also a minimum value of \(Q\), \(Q_{\min}\) that is determined by the divergence of the incident beam and the distance and shielding of the detector. Hence in the transform from \(S(Q)\) to \(g(r)\) the limits are \(Q_{\min}\) and \(Q_{\max}\) that are determined by experimental constraints.
The maximum measured value, \(Q_{\max}\), determines the real-space resolution that can be achieved after Fourier transformation. Higher values of \(Q_{\max}\) generally allow finer structural detail to be resolved.
The minimum measured value, \(Q_{\min}\), determines the largest structural length scales that can be probed. Structural features occurring below \(Q_{\min}\) cannot be measured directly.
As a result, diffraction experiments always involve a compromise between access to long-range structure (low \(Q\)) and high real-space resolution (high \(Q\)).

title: 13  Measurements in reciprocal space
text:
13.5 Partial Structure Factors
As we noted previously, the discussion so far has only considered mono-atomic systems - a very limited case! In reality we deal with materials that contain more than one atom type and hence we need a way to describe the arrangements of different types of atom around each other, i.e., how do we interpret the diffraction pattern from a multicomponent system? Well, we can extend our idea of the radial distribution function and introduce the idea of a partial radial distribution function, \(g_{\alpha\beta}(r)\), which may be described as the radial distribution function for the arrangement of atoms of type \(\beta\) around those of type \(\alpha\). We note also that \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) can represent the same atom type. Take for example a glass such as germanium dioxide (\(GeO_2\)). We can define four partial radial distribution functions, \(g_{GeGe}(r)\) describing the distribution of the germanium atoms around a germanium atom at the origin, \(g_{OO}(r)\) describing the distribution of oxygen atoms around an oxygen atom at the origin and \(g_{GeO}(r)\) describing the distribution of oxygen atoms around a germanium atom at the origin and vice versa (\(g_{OGe}(r)\)). With a little thought we can also see that \(g_{GeO}(r)=g_{OGe}(r)\) so that for our binary system we only need 3 partial radial distribution functions to describe the structure. Extending the arguments we used previously, we may then define the partial structure \(S_{\alpha\beta}(Q)\) as,
\[S_{\alpha\beta}(Q)=1+ \frac{4\pi\rho}{Q}\int_0^{\infty}r(g_{\alpha\beta}(r)-1)\sin(Qr)dr\]
for which the inverse transform is,
\[g_{\alpha\beta}(r)=1+\frac{1}{2\pi\rho r}\int_0^{\infty}Q(S_{\alpha\beta}(Q)-1)\sin(Qr)dQ\]

title: 13  Measurements in reciprocal space
text:
13.6 Diffraction from multicomponent systems
Experimentally, we do not measure the individual partial structure factors directly. Instead, the diffraction pattern is a weighted sum of all pair correlations.
For neutron diffraction:
\[
F^N(Q)=\sum_{\alpha}\sum_{\beta}c_\alpha c_\beta b_\alpha b_\beta \left[S_{\alpha\beta}(Q)-1\right]
\]
where \(c_\alpha\) is the atomic concentration and \(b_\alpha\) is the neutron scattering length.
For X-ray diffraction, the neutron scattering lengths are replaced by the X-ray form factors.
Consequently, a single diffraction experiment generally cannot uniquely determine all partial structure factors. Additional information or additional measurements are required.

title: 13  Measurements in reciprocal space
text:
13.7 Neutron diffraction and isotope substitution
One of the most powerful approaches for obtaining partial structural information is neutron diffraction with isotope substitution (NDIS).
Unlike X-rays, neutrons scatter from atomic nuclei. The neutron scattering length depends strongly on isotope, while the overall chemistry of the material remains essentially unchanged.
For example, the different isotopes of germanium possess different neutron scattering lengths. By preparing chemically identical samples containing different isotopes and measuring their diffraction patterns, different weightings of the same underlying partial structure factors can be obtained.
Combining these measurements provides sufficient information to isolate the individual partial structure factors, such as
\[
S_{GeGe}(Q),\qquad S_{GeO}(Q), \qquad S_{OO}(Q).
\]
NDIS has played an important role in determining the structures of liquids and glasses, although its use is limited by the availability and cost of isotopically enriched materials, as well as the difficulty of extending the method to systems containing many atomic species.

title: 13  Measurements in reciprocal space
text:
13.8 Summary and keypoints
As we approach atomic sizes attempts to measure structural properties in real space (\(g(r)\)) become harder and harder. In this regime the main tools for measuring structure are X-ray and neutron diffraction and perhaps electron diffraction in certain cases.
In diffraction experiments important factors to consider are,

the wavelength of the x-ray or neutrons,
the maximum and minimum accessible \(Q\) value compared to the length scales being probed,
the accessibility of the source (central facilities needed?),
cost and availability of isotopes.

title: 14  Entropy matters
text:
14.1 Systems and definitions
Most of the matter around us does not simply fit within the idealized pictures of crystalline solids or simple liquids: examples include colloids, polymers, surfactants, liquid crystals, foams, gels, and biological materials such as proteins, DNA, and cell membranes.
As Philip Anderson put it in a famous essay, more is different (Anderson 1972): when many simple units interact, collective properties emerge that cannot be understood by studying the individual components alone.
This means that cellular life itself (the very constituents that make us) obeys principles that go beyond the standard patterns of conventional solid-state physics.
This branch of physics is called soft condensed matter physics, or macromolecular physics, or the physics of complex fluids. Specifically, soft matter refers to an area of condensed matter focused on systems that can be easily deformed.
In this course, we will emphasize the fact that many such systems are not crystalline: thermal noise and disordered configurations play a key role in their phase behavior, and hence we think of them as complex disordered systems.
While we often think about problems in physics as a matter of energy minimization, in soft-matter physics a key role is played by fluctuations. Typically (but not exclusively) these are thermal fluctuations. This means that entropy and not only the energy from the interactions plays a key role.
This is because soft matter systems are typically composed of many microscopic constituents in contact with an environment. The appropriate description of the macroscopic state of such systems is therefore statistical and uses the language of statistical mechanics. The relevant energy, therefore, is the free energy of the statistical ensemble representative of the system under consideration. For example, in the canonical ensemble, this is the Helmholtz free energy
\[F = U-TS\]
where \(U\) is the internal energy, \(T\) the temperature and \(S\) is the entropy of the system. Therefore, in a broader sense, soft matter is the physics of those systems for which the internal energy and the entropy are on comparable scales.
Per particle, the free energy reads \(f = u - Ts\). The entropy approximately counts the number of arrangements per particle, \(s = \dfrac{k_B}{N}\ln\Omega\): for hundreds of arrangements per particle one has \(s = O(1)\,k_B\), so that the entropic term \(Ts\) is of the order of \(k_BT\).
In other words, fluctuations of the internal energy per constituent are on the same scale as thermal fluctuations:
\[\Delta u \sim k_BT \]
where \(k_B\) is the Boltzmann constant and \(\Delta u\) indicates standard deviations from the average internal energy per constituent.

title: 14  Entropy matters
text:
14.1.1 Elementary constituents and energy scales
Soft matter covers a wide spectrum of deformable systems. Each is constituted of many parts. Each is deformable because the interactions amongst such parts are weak compared to the perturbing forces (e.g. thermal fluctuations or mechanical loading).
In hard condensed matter, the elementary constituents are the atoms themselves, eventually with their subatomic particles. Between atoms, the scale of the interaction energies is in the 0.1 to 10 eV: for example the carbon-carbon covalent bond is approximately 3.6 eV.
The main units of soft matter are not atoms. They are instead themselves aggregates of atoms such as:

colloids, micrometer- to nanometer-sized particles dispersed in a fluid.
polymers, macromolecules composed of long chains such as DNA, proteins, plastics
surfactants, molecules with polar head and tails that lead to the spontaneous formation of structures such as bilayers (e.g. the cellular membrane).

Amongst such units, the dominating forces of soft matter are much weaker than in hard condensed matter:

Van der Waals interaction energies are of the order of 0.001-0.01 eV
weak interactions such as hydrogen-bonds are typically in the 0.01-0.2 eV range
the thermal energy at room temperature is \(k_B T \approx 0.025 eV\) (check it for yourself)

At the microscopic level, all these interactions have essentially one source: the electrostatic force. However, this information is practically of no use when we want to understand how the units of soft matter come together to give rise to macroscopic properties of soft matter systems, such as their elastic properties, their viscosities, their plasticity. In fact, the emphasis on the atomistic details of the various units is fundamentally misleading: atomistically very different objects (e.g. colloids and micelles) can in fact share very similar macroscopic behaviours.
Therefore, theories of soft matter leverage the concept of coarse-graining, rooted in the renormalisation group notions explored earlier. Coarse-graining means integrating out the unimportant degrees of freedom and only describing the units in terms of a few important parameters. For example, instead of taking a full atomistic representation of the DNA we may want to focus on the fact that structurally it is a long chain with specific bending energies: we may want to include the fact that it is formed by a double helix but we may not want to specifically construct every single atom in the sugar chain that forms the backbone. An example of DNA coarse graining is provided by the successful model oxDNA (see picture below):



oxDNA model: (a) Base structure on one strand; (b) planarity of the bonding; (c) an example of the resulting double strand.








NoteCoarse graining





Coarse graining is often motivated by intuition, experimental insights or a simple desire of simplification. It allows for a multi-scale description of the problem which permits to describe large systems and long time scales.
Nonetheless, coarse-graining can also be made mathematically rigorous. For example, rigorous coarse graining in statistical mechanics can be performed by projecting the dynamics onto a relevant and an irrelevant (fluctuating) part, in the so called Mori-Zwanzig formalism (Mori 1965).





14.1.2 Classes of systems
In our exploration of soft matter we will focus on five main classes of systems which display different physics:

colloidal dispersions
polymeric systems
liquid crystals 
arrested systems
active matter


Colloidal dispersions
Colloidal dispersions are systems where small particles, typically in the nanometer to micrometer range, are dispersed in a continuous medium (a solvent). Prototypical colloids are spherical particles of various sizes (e.g. as those present in paint) but colloidal science has achieved a high degree of sophistication, with colloidal particles with various different shapes and interactions.
Colloids are often thought as big atoms: they exhibit Brownian motion, can form ordered structures (colloidal crystals), and display phase transitions similar to atomic systems. However, their larger size and slower dynamics make them ideal for studying phenomena that are difficult to observe in atomic systems.


Polymeric systems
Polymer physics is a field on its own. Polymers are macromolecules composed of repeating structural units (monomers) connected by covalent bonds. Their unique properties arise from their string-like structure and the interplay between entropic and energetic contributions.
Polymers can be classified into two main categories:

Synthetic polymers, including plastics (e.g., polyethylene, polystyrene) and synthetic rubbers.
Biopolymers, such as polymers like DNA, RNA, and proteins.

Compared to colloids, polymers have distinctive characteristics common to all chain-like molecules, such as their topological constraints due to the fact that two polymers cannot cross each other (a phenomenon known as polymer entanglement).


Liquid crystals
When we take soft matter units that are highly anisotropic (e.g. elongate in particular directions) thermal fluctuations and high packing lead to equilibrium states with a degree of order that is intermediate between the complete disorder of a liquid and the long-ranged, three-dimensional order of a crystal.
Such states are referred to as liquid crystal and can be described successfully with continuum free energy theories that take into account the symmetries of the order parameters.
Components that form liquid crystals are called mesogens and include highly anisotropic organic macromolecules (as used in liquid crystal displays), rod-like molecules or polymeric aggregates, as well as disk-shaped molecules and particles(such as triphenylene and derivatives).



Arrested systems
We have stressed that the thermal energy is distinctive of soft matter systems. It would be then natural to assume that as we reduce the temperature, we should converge readily to the solid state physics of crystalline solids. In fact, on the way to low temperatures, the lack of long-range order of most soft-matter systems has important consequences: many such systems find themselves trapped in states that are not corresponding to the global energy minimum (i.e. the crystal) and instead display non trivial mechanisms of structural relaxation. These systems are disordered a bit like liquids, but share various mechanical properties, such as emergent rigidity, elasticity and plasticity.
Examples of arrested systems include:

Glasses, such as silica glass or metallic glasses, where the system is kinetically trapped in a disordered state.
Gels, which are networks of interconnected particles or polymers that span the entire system, providing rigidity despite being mostly liquid.

These systems are arrested as their relaxation towards equilibrium is so slow that it is longer than any observable timescales. This makes them fundamentally out-of-equilibrium systems, escaping from an ordinary description in terms of equilibrium statistical mechanics.


Active matter
Active matter refers to systems composed of units that consume energy to generate motion or mechanical stresses. Unlike passive systems, active matter is inherently out of equilibrium due to the continuous energy input at the microscopic level. Examples include:

Biological systems, such as bacterial colonies, cell tissues, and flocks of birds.
Synthetic systems, like self-propelled colloids or active gels.

The study of active matter focuses on understanding how individual activity leads to emergent collective behaviors, such as swarming, clustering, or pattern formation, often described using hydrodynamic theories or agent-based models.

title: 15  Colloids
text:
15.1 Kinds of colloids
Colloids are mixtures where one substance is dispersed throughout another. They consist of particles that are larger than typical atoms/molecules but small enough to remain suspended without settling. Examples include milk, fog, and paint.
Colloids can be classified based on the state of the dispersed phase and the dispersion medium. Depending on the particular mixture, one can obtain a wide variety of soft materials, with unique mechanical, optical, and thermal properties.
Clearly, colloidal materials form an incredibly diverse class, and surround us in our everyday lives. Here are some visual examples from the table above:
The IUPAC definition of colloids is based on the idea that the particles are dispersed in a medium, creating a subdivision at the colloidal scale, which is approximately 1 nm to 1 µm.
The small size of colloids means that they are constantly subject to collisions with the atoms/molecules/particles of the medium, triggered by thermal fluctuations. Due to this, the colloids undergo Brownian motion. For each particle, the amount of energy received from the medium is of the order of \(k_B T\) (the reference energy scale of soft matter). This energy can be compared with the potential energy associated with a displacement of a particle radius to produce a dimensionless number, the gravitational Péclet number
\[{\rm Pe}_g = \dfrac{\Delta m g R}{k_B T}\]
where \(R\) is the radius of the colloid, \(g\) is the acceleration due to gravity, and \(\Delta m\) is the buoyant mass, which for a spherical colloid is expressed as \(\Delta m = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\Delta\rho R^3\), with \(\Delta \rho\) being the density difference between the particle and the dispersion medium (the solvent). We have a colloidal suspension only when \({\rm Pe}_g \lesssim 1\), i.e. when Brownian motion is only marginally perturbed by the effects of gravity.
